Issued at 136 AM MDT Sun Nov 1 2026

The weather has cooperated for the most part for evening activities 
for Halloween. We are now entering what I call the 151 days (or 152 
if it is a leap year) of winter in western and central Wyoming. This 
is when we usually start expecting more wintery precipitation than 
rain. I say usually because the past couple of winters have been 
unusually warm and dry. We will have the precipitation, and there 
will be some snow, but not really in the lower elevations. Going to 
try something different tonight with the discussion, I will discuss 
the overall weather pattern over the next couple of days first with 
the players. Then, I will focus on the three main impacts, 
precipitation amounts, potential snowfall and amounts and finally 
potential for strong to high wind in portions of the area.

The low that will be bringing the precipitation today is now moving 
onshore in northern California and will open a trough crossing the 
Rockies late tonight and into tomorrow. The latest model trends have 
been downward somewhat though with QPF, with the bulk remaining to 
the south over Utah, Colorado and Arizona. We will see some here 
though, with the heaviest precipitation in the west through midnight 
tonight, tapering off after midnight after the trough axis passes 
through the area. For areas East of the Divide, although there will 
be some showers around this morning, the most numerous should be 
tonight through Monday morning. Lee cyclogenesis will occur over 
eastern Colorado late today and then the low will strengthen as it 
moves northeastward into the Northern Plains states. This will 
likely bring some wrap around moisture that will keep precipitation 
going somewhat longer. However, it will also introduce a dry slot 
that could keep amounts down somewhere. And this complicates the 
rain and snow forecast somewhat. And finally, with the deepening 
flow, the pressure gradient will tighten across the area. This will 
bring the likelihood of strong wind to much of the area and 
potentially high wind to portions of Johnson County. These main 
impacts should end Monday evening as the low moves away to the east.
Now for the individual forecast elements.

Precipitation amounts...As was stated earlier, these have trended 
down somewhat with core of the moisture remaining to the south. 
However, all areas should see some precipitation. The wettest areas 
at this time look to be 1) Far southern Wyoming, which will be 
closer to the core of the deeper moisture; 2) The western facing 
slopes in the western mountains with a period of favorable 
orographic flow and 3) Favored northerly upslope flow areas East of 
the Divide like the Wind River Basin south of Riverton and the 
Lander Foothills, around Casper, the southern end of the Bighorn 
Basin and the eastern Bighorns. As a counter, the least amounts 
would be in 1) far northern Wyoming, which will be away from the 
core moisture and 2) Areas of downslope, like the eastern Bighorn 
Basin, the northern Wind River Basin and the Green River Basin. 
However, there are still model differences on the placement of the 
heaviest rain and the potential dry slot. Other differences are with 
the amount of wrap around, as some have it further west than others.
As for amounts, most areas have at least a 1 in 2 chance of a 
quarter inch of QPF or more, with the exception of the 
aforementioned downslope areas. As for greatest chance of three 
quarters of an inch or more, this would be mainly in the 
aforementioned upslope areas. Some areas will likely see more than 
an inch of QPF through the system though. Most should end by sunset 
Monday, with all precipitation finished by sunrise on Tuesday. 
CONFIDENCE IN AMOUNTS...Moderate to low.

Snow...For the most part, this looks like only the mountains for 
this. Snow levels remain fairly high through this afternoon, ranging 
from 8000 feet in the far west to 9500 to 10000 feet in eastern 
portions of the area. The cooler air then works in as flow turns 
north, falling as low as minus 3 to minus 4 by Monday afternoon. 
This would drop snow levels down to 7000 to as low as 6500 feet. 
However, the deepest moisture would be out of the area by then. 
There could be some snowflakes mixed in or possibly a brief period 
of wet snow in a place like Dubois, Meeteetse or areas along US 20 
26 like Hiland, but accumulation would be slim to none. Most 
mountains will see at least some accumulation though. The amount we 
are most concerned with is 6 inches, which is needed for most 
advisories. In the western mountains, this is largely restricted to 
the highest elevations, so we will not issue highlights here. The 
southern Absarokas have a 1 in 2 chance, but these are in areas with 
no population and no impact. The Wind River Range does but we 
already have an advisory for the western Wind River Range. I thought 
about extending it to the eastern Winds but will hold off for now.
